label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
**Why I'm keeping the busing project**

Most of you already know this from the group chat, but here's the short version for anyone who doesn't. A parent emailed my principal to complain about the oral history project I do with my juniors, and cc'd a school committee member for good measure. Dr. Halvorsen would like me to quietly drop it. I'm not going to.

Jess texted me last night, and the gist was: it's one assignment, don't torch your job over it. About half the chat agreed with her. I started typing a reply, got to the fourth paragraph, and realized I'd rather say it once in full than in fifteen pieces. So this is for everybody, but Jess, it's mostly for you.

First, the project, since some of you have only heard me describe it after two beers. Both my US History II sections do it. Each kid interviews someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston during busing, 1974 to 1976. They turn in a ten minute recording and a two page reflection. I've done it for four years at Cobb Street, and until this fall nobody had complained.

The email said the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents."

I want to be fair to this parent, because I think she's half right, and the half she's right about matters. A sixteen year old sitting across from her grandfather with a phone recording and a grade attached is under pressure, even if I never meant it that way. If a kid doesn't want to ask their family about 1974, or the family doesn't want to be asked, there has to be a way through the assignment that doesn't go through their kitchen table. There wasn't one. That's on me, and I should have fixed it years ago.

So I'm fixing it. Starting now there's a second option. A student can interview a librarian or an archivist who works with this material, or they can work from the recorded interviews from past years, with permission from the people in them. They do the same reflection for the same grade, and nobody has to interview a relative. That's what I'm bringing to the meeting with Halvorsen and the parent on Thursday the 19th at 3:15. I'm not going in there to fight her. I'm going in to tell her she had a point and show her what I did about it.

What I won't do is make the whole thing disappear, and that's the part I owe you an explanation for.

In 2023 a student I'll call D. interviewed his grandmother. It turned out she drove a school bus in Southie in '74. She had never told anyone in the family, not her kids and not him, until he asked her for a homework assignment. He played forty seconds of it for the class. When it ended nobody said a word for what felt like a full minute, and if you've ever stood in front of a room of juniors you know how rare that is.

Last year a girl found out from her interview that her uncle threw rocks at a bus. She was upset, really upset, and we talked after class twice. I won't pretend that was comfortable for either of us. But her reflection was the best thing I read all year. She didn't excuse him or disown him. She worked out, on paper, how to hold both things about a person she loves. I can't teach that from the front of the room. I've tried.

That's what the parent means by reopening wounds, and I get it. But the textbook gives all of this one paragraph. It gets one paragraph, in a book these kids read in Boston, about the streets they take to school and the buildings they sit in. If I drop the project, what replaces it is that paragraph and a quiz.

I do think the kids who are uncomfortable are often the ones who need it most. I also know I don't get to force anyone, and I'd be a worse teacher if I thought I did. Offering it is my job. Requiring a kid to go dig through their own family is not. I had that line in the wrong place before, and the alternate option moves it to where it should have been.

Now, Jess. You're not wrong that I could get burned, and I don't want you to think I waved that off. I've had tenure since 2021, so nobody's firing me over this. But Halvorsen still makes my schedule and still decides who teaches AP, and there are plenty of ways to make a teacher's year miserable without ever putting anything in writing. You know that better than most people. We figured out how schools really work together, back when we were student teaching in the same building in 2012 and had no idea what we were doing. You got out in 2019, and now you sit on the HR side of the table at a biotech in Cambridge and watch how these things go for people. When you tell me to be careful, I know it's coming from someone who has seen it from both ends.

So I'll say the embarrassing part. I'm scared, a little. I'm not being brave about this. I've been running Thursday's meeting in my head at two in the morning, and in most versions I say something stupid. If I come out of it with five sections of freshmen and a lunch duty, you get to say you told me so, and I'll buy the drinks.

But I keep thinking about D.'s grandmother carrying that for almost fifty years until a kid with an assignment asked. If I quietly drop this because one email got cc'd to the right person, I'm telling my students that the way to deal with the hard part of where you live is to not bring it up, and this city has been dealing with it that way for as long as I've been alive.

I'm not asking you to agree. You might read all this and still think it's one assignment and I'm being stubborn, and you might be right. I just wanted you to know it wasn't a reflex. I thought about what you said, and I'm still thinking about it.

I'll text you Thursday as soon as I'm out of the meeting. Keep your phone on.
